{{Short description|Restricted type of addition chain}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Lucas chain''' is a restricted type of [[addition chain]], named for the French mathematician [[Édouard Lucas]]. It is a [[sequence]] 
:<math>a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots</math>
that satisfies {{math|1=''a''<sub>0</sub>=1}}, and, for each {{math|''k'' > 0}},
: <math>a_k = a_i + a_j,</math>
and either
: <math>a_i = a_j \text{ or } \vert a_i - a_j \vert = a_m </math>
for some {{math|1=''i'', ''j'', ''m'' < ''k''}}.<ref name="G169">Guy (2004) p.169</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|title=Lucas Chain|url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/LucasChain.html|access-date=2020-08-11|website=mathworld.wolfram.com|language=en}}</ref>

The sequence of powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...) and the [[Fibonacci sequence]] (with a slight adjustment of the starting point 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ...) are simple examples of Lucas chains.

Lucas chains were introduced by [[Peter Montgomery (mathematician)|Peter Montgomery]] in 1983.<ref>Kutz (2002)</ref> They are analogous to [[addition chain]]s, in that just as an addition chain {{mvar|A}} that ends with {{mvar|n}} allows for evaluating {{mvar|a<sup>n</sup>}} in {{math|1=len(''A'')}} steps, a Lucas chain {{mvar|C}} that ends with {{mvar|n}} allow for evaluating the [[Lucas sequence]] terms {{math|1={<span style="margin-left:-0.08em">''U''</span>, ''V''&hairsp;}<sub>''n''</sub>&thinsp;(''P'', ''Q'')}} in {{math|1=len(''C'')}} steps.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Ching-Te |last2=Chang |first2=Chin-Chen |last3=Lin |first3=Chu-Hsing |title=A method for computing Lucas sequences |journal=Computers & Mathematics with Applications |date=December 1999 |volume=38 |issue=11-12 |pages=187–196 |doi=10.1016/S0898-1221(99)00297-7}}</ref>

Just like the addition chain, a basic method for computing a Lucas chain that ends with {{mvar|n}} is via the ''binary method'', similar to [[exponentiation by squaring]]. This gives a chain length of {{math|1=''O''(log ''n'')}}.
Shorter chains can be obtained using a range of other methods such as Montgomery's PRAC. Because the process of finding a better chain is expensive, good chains are usually precomputed.<ref name=PZ06>{{cite book |last1=Zimmermann |first1=Paul |last2=Dodson |first2=Bruce |chapter=20 Years of ECM |title=Algorithmic Number Theory |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=2006 |volume=4076 |pages=525–542 |doi=10.1007/11792086_37|isbn=978-3-540-36075-9 |chapter-url=https://members.loria.fr/PZimmermann/papers/ecm-submitted.pdf}} [https://inria.hal.science/inria-00070192v2 HAL]</ref>
DJ Bernstein mentions a number of Lucas chain-based schemes in 2017.<ref>{{Citation| last1 = Bernstein| first1 = Daniel J.| last2 = Lange| first2 = Tanja| title = Montgomery curves and the Montgomery ladder| access-date = 2025-11-06| date = 2017| url = https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/293}}</ref>{{rp|at=&sect;4.8.2}}

If {{math|1=''L''(''n'')}} is the length of the shortest Lucas chain for {{mvar|n}}, then Kutz has shown that most {{mvar|n}} do not have {{math|1=''L'' < (1-ε) log<sub>φ</sub>(''n'')}}, where φ is the [[Golden ratio]].<ref name=G169/>
